mainTopic: Hearing one's own words and pronouncing carefully in קריאת שמע and other מצות
overview: The גמרא keeps asking whether the משנה that excludes a חרש from reading the מגילה can follow רבי יהודה, who holds that קריאת שמע said without hearing counts בדיעבד. After several back-and-forth arguments, it shows that the whole משנה can be רבי יהודה's if it speaks of two kinds of קטן. Two ברייתות then seem to conflict: one lets a deaf person separate תרומה even לכתחילה, and the other says silent ברכת המזון counts only בדיעבד. The גמרא solves this in two ways, using רבי יהודה's teacher רבי אלעזר בן עזריה and רבי מאיר. רב חסדא rules that לכתחילה one must hear his own קריאת שמע, but בדיעבד he is יוצא. רב יוסף's statement is corrected to say that in other מצות everyone agrees one is יוצא without hearing. Next come rulings and teachings about reading carefully: be lenient in both disputes of the משנה, write the whole פרשה in a מזוזה, and pause between words that run together. Along the way there is an אגדה about תחיית המתים, and a teaching that careful reading of שמע cools גיהנם. A new teaching of רבי חמא ברבי חנינא begins at the end and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Maybe the משנה follows רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the משנה excluding a חרש could follow רבי יהודה. It would only mean a חרש should not read לכתחילה, but his reading still counts בדיעבד.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps the משנה follows רבי יהודה. It only means a חרש should not read in the first place, but if he already read, it is fine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the claim that the משנה follows רבי יוסי. It offers another way to read it: as רבי יהודה's view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה holds that saying the words without hearing them is a problem only לכתחילה. If the משנה only means 'a חרש should not read in the first place,' it fits רבי יהודה. Then the proof for רבי יוסי falls apart.

keyTerms.meaning: from the outset / ideally, before the act
after the fact / once it was already done
it is fine / it is valid

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רבי יהודה says a חרש may read whenever he wants. The suggestion is only that the act still counts once it is done. Ideally, he should still not read.

phrases.english: Perhaps it is Rabbi Yehuda,
phrases.notes: Suggests a different author for the משנה.

phrases.english: and it is only from the outset that [a deaf person] may not [read],
phrases.notes: Limits the משנה's exclusion to ideal practice.

phrases.english: but after the fact, it is fine.
phrases.notes: If he already read, it counts.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the earlier attempt to attribute the משנה to רבי יוסי.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the משנה excluding a חרש must follow רבי יוסי.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה's exclusion might mean only לכתחילה. That would fit רבי יהודה, so there is no proof for רבי יוסי.

steps.title: A deaf person is compared to an imbecile and a minor
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the suggestion. The משנה lists a חרש together with a שוטה and a קטן, whose reading does not count even בדיעבד, so a חרש's reading also does not count בדיעבד.
steps.simpleTranslation: That cannot be. The משנה puts a חרש in the same list as a שוטה and a קטן. Their reading does not count even after the fact, so a חרש's reading also does not count even after the fact.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the original claim. It points to how the משנה groups the three people together.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone agrees a שוטה and a קטן are completely unable to read for others, even after the fact. Since a חרש is listed right next to them, his exclusion should be just as complete. That fits רבי יוסי, not רבי יהודה.

keyTerms.meaning: it cannot enter your mind (that idea is impossible)
a minor, not yet obligated in מצוות
a deaf person (here: one who can speak but cannot hear)

phrases.english: This could not enter your mind,
phrases.notes: Strong rejection of the suggestion.

phrases.english: for it teaches a deaf person alongside an imbecile and a minor, [showing he is] similar to them.
phrases.notes: The proof comes from their grouping in one list.

phrases.aramaic: מָה שׁוֹטֶה וְקָטָן דִּיעֲבַד נָמֵי לָא —
phrases.english: Just as an imbecile and a minor [are] not [valid] even after the fact,
phrases.notes: Their exclusion is total.

phrases.english: so too a deaf person [is] not [valid] even after the fact.
phrases.notes: The same rule is applied to the חרש.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Proof from the grouping of cases in the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The exclusion of a חרש might be only לכתחילה, like רבי יהודה.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because a חרש is grouped with a שוטה and a קטן, his exclusion applies even בדיעבד, like רבי יוסי.

steps.title: Each case may have its own rule
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof from the list. Each case in the list could keep its own separate rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe this one has its rule and that one has its rule. Being listed together does not make their rules identical.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down the proof from step 2. Being listed together does not prove the same level of exclusion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A שוטה and a קטן could be invalid even בדיעבד, while a חרש is invalid only לכתחילה. All three still share a list, because none of them should read in the first place. So the door to רבי יהודה is open again.

keyTerms.meaning: this one as it is, and that one as it is (each case keeps its own rule)

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying a חרש is not in the same category as the others. All three are excluded. The only question is how strong the exclusion is: לכתחילה only, or even בדיעבד.

phrases.english: And perhaps this one is as it is
phrases.notes: The שוטה and קטן keep their full exclusion.

phrases.english: and that one is as it is.
phrases.notes: The חרש may have a milder exclusion.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the answer given in step 2.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof from the grouping, not the final attribution itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Listing cases together does not require them to share the same level of invalidity.

steps.title: The first clause cannot be רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a new argument. The סיפא says 'רבי יהודה permits a קטן,' which shows the רישא is not רבי יהודה's view.
steps.simpleTranslation: Can you really explain the first part as רבי יהודה's view? The last part says 'רבי יהודה permits a קטן.' That shows the first part is not רבי יהודה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the idea of step 1 from a new angle. It looks at the structure of the משנה itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the רישא were already רבי יהודה, there would be no reason to bring his disagreement separately in the סיפא. Naming רבי יהודה at the end shows the anonymous first clause is a different תנא. So the רישא cannot be explained as רבי יהודה's 'לכתחילה only' approach.

keyTerms.meaning: can you really establish/explain it (as following)?
the latter clause of a משנה
the first clause of a משנה

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a classic גמרא tool. When a תנא's name appears as a dissent in the סיפא, the unnamed רישא is usually a different opinion.
steps.whatToRemember: The suggestion that the משנה follows רבי יהודה is now challenged by the משנה's own structure. רבי יהודה is quoted as disagreeing in the סיפא, so the רישא is someone else.

phrases.english: And can you establish it as following Rabbi Yehuda?
phrases.notes: Rhetorical challenge to step 1.

phrases.english: But from what is taught in the latter clause:
phrases.notes: Introduces the evidence from the end of the משנה.

phrases.english: 'Rabbi Yehuda deems a minor fit,'
phrases.notes: Quote from the משנה in מגילה.

phrases.aramaic: מִכְּלָל דְּרֵישָׁא לָאו רַבִּי יְהוּדָה הִיא?!
phrases.english: it follows by inference that the first clause is not Rabbi Yehuda?!
phrases.notes: The anonymous first clause must be a different תנא.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 3 reopened the רבי יהודה option, this step challenges it from a new angle.
steps.kashyaTarget: The suggestion (step 1) that the רישא of the משנה follows רבי יהודה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The סיפא quotes רבי יהודה as disagreeing, which implies the anonymous רישא is not his view.

steps.title: The whole משנה can still follow רבי יהודה, because it speaks about two kinds of minors
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof from the סיפא. It says the entire משנה can be רבי יהודה's, because it speaks about two kinds of קטן and is missing some words.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe the whole משנה is רבי יהודה's view. There are two types of קטן, and the משנה is missing words. It really teaches this: Everyone may read the מגילה except a חרש, a שוטה, and a קטן. When is this said? About a קטן who has not reached חינוך. But a קטן who has reached חינוך may read even לכתחילה. These are the words of רבי יהודה, because רבי יהודה permits a קטן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 4. It shows that the line 'רבי יהודה permits a קטן' does not prove the רישא belongs to someone else.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 4 the סיפא looked like רבי יהודה was arguing with the רישא. Now the גמרא fills in missing words. The רישא excludes only a young קטן who has not reached חינוך, and the סיפא adds that an older קטן is allowed. So רבי יהודה is explaining the רישא, not disagreeing with it, and the whole משנה can be his.

keyTerms.meaning: Two types (here, two kinds of קטן)
The text is missing words, and this is what it really teaches
In what case is this said? (a phrase that limits the rule)
Reached the age of training in מצוות

steps.confusionAlert: The rewritten משנה is not a different text. The גמרא is saying the משנה we have leaves out words, and it fills them in so that the רישא and סיפא fit together under one author.

phrases.english: But perhaps the whole of it is Rabbi Yehuda
and there are two types of minor,
and it is missing words, and this is what it teaches:
All are fit to read the Megillah,
except a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor.
In what case is this said?
With a minor who has not reached training age,
phrases.notes: This young minor is the one the רישא excludes.

phrases.english: but a minor who has reached training age
is fit even from the outset,
these are the words of Rabbi Yehuda,
for Rabbi Yehuda deems a minor fit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects Step 4's proof that the רישא is not רבי יהודה.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the inference from the סיפא's wording.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Step 4 assumed the סיפא disagrees with the רישא. It can instead be an explanation of the רישא that splits קטן into two cases.

steps.title: Questioning whether רבי יהודה really holds 'only after the fact,' using a ברייתא about separating תרומה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether it is right that רבי יהודה holds 'בדיעבד yes, לכתחילה no.' It brings a ברייתא that lets a deaf person who speaks separate תרומה even לכתחילה.
steps.simpleTranslation: How did you set up the משנה? According to רבי יהודה, that בדיעבד yes but לכתחילה no? But what about the ברייתא taught by רבי יהודה the son of רבי שמעון בן פזי: a deaf person who speaks but does not hear may separate תרומה even לכתחילה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new challenge. It questions the whole idea built in Steps 1–5, that רבי יהודה says a חרש's action counts only בדיעבד. This step sets up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everything so far assumed that, for רבי יהודה, words a person says without hearing them count only בדיעבד. A person separating תרומה says a ברכה, and a deaf person cannot hear his own ברכה. Yet this ברייתא lets him separate תרומה even לכתחילה, which does not fit 'בדיעבד only.'

keyTerms.meaning: How did you set it up? Whose view did you assign it to?
After the fact (it counts if it was already done)
From the outset (one may do it this way in the first place)
A deaf person who can speak but cannot hear
Separates תרומה (the portion of produce given to a כהן)

steps.confusionAlert: The רבי יהודה who teaches this ברייתא (the son of רבי שמעון בן פזי) is a later teacher. He is NOT the תנא רבי יהודה whose opinion is being discussed.

phrases.english: How did you establish it? According to Rabbi Yehuda,
that after the fact yes, but from the outset no?
But what about that which was taught by

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן פַּזִּי,
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi:
A deaf person who speaks but does not hear
may separate terumah from the outset,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts that the משנה can be רבי יהודה's, then questions the 'בדיעבד only' assumption about רבי יהודה himself.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption that רבי יהודה holds 'בדיעבד yes, לכתחילה no' for words said without hearing.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא allows a deaf person to separate תרומה לכתחילה, even though he cannot hear his own ברכה.

steps.title: The תרומה ברייתא seems to fit neither רבי יהודה nor רבי יוסי
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whose view the ברייתא is. It fits neither רבי יהודה (only בדיעבד) nor רבי יוסי (not even בדיעבד).
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose view is it? It is neither רבי יהודה nor רבי יוסי. If it is רבי יהודה, he says בדיעבד yes but לכתחילה no. If it is רבי יוסי, he says it does not count even בדיעבד!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sharpens the challenge. The ברייתא allowing a deaf person to separate תרומה לכתחילה has no author who fits it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two known views about saying words without hearing them. רבי יהודה allows it only after the fact, and רבי יוסי does not allow it at all. A ruling that allows it even לכתחילה matches neither view, so something in our understanding must be wrong. The implied suggestion is that רבי יהודה actually allows it even לכתחילה.

keyTerms.meaning: The תנא who holds that words said without hearing do not count even בדיעבד
If this ... if that (testing each option)

phrases.aramaic: מַנִּי? לָא רַבִּי יְהוּדָה וְלָא רַבִּי יוֹסֵי.
phrases.english: Whose is it? Neither Rabbi Yehuda nor Rabbi Yosei.
If Rabbi Yehuda,
after the fact yes, from the outset no.
If Rabbi Yosei,
even after the fact no!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַנִּי? לָא רַבִּי יְהוּדָה וְלָא רַבִּי יוֹסֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the challenge begun in Step 6 by showing the ברייתא has no author.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that רבי יהודה holds 'בדיעבד only.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If רבי יהודה holds 'בדיעבד only,' a ברייתא allowing it לכתחילה becomes authorless. So perhaps רבי יהודה allows it even לכתחילה.
steps.whyThisMatters: If רבי יהודה allows it even לכתחילה, then the explanation of the מגילה משנה built in Steps 1–5 would need rethinking.

steps.title: Pushback: if רבי יהודה allows it from the outset, whose view is the ברייתא about silent ברכת המזון?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back on the idea that רבי יהודה allows it even לכתחילה. A ברייתא says not to say ברכת המזון silently, but if one did, he is יוצא. Whose view would that be?
steps.simpleTranslation: But then what? Does רבי יהודה allow it even לכתחילה? Then what about the ברייתא: A person should not say ברכת המזון in his heart, but if he did, he is יוצא. Whose view is that?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the new suggestion from Step 7. It brings a ברייתא that clearly holds 'בדיעבד yes, לכתחילה no' and asks who could be its author. The answer comes in the next part of the גמרא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא about ברכת המזון fits exactly the view 'בדיעבד only.' It cannot be רבי יוסי, who says not even בדיעבד. If רבי יהודה allows it even לכתחילה, this ברייתא would have no author either. So both possible views of רבי יהודה leave one ברייתא without an author.

keyTerms.meaning: But rather, what? (pushing back on a suggestion)
In his heart: silently, without saying it out loud

steps.whatToRemember: There are now two ברייתות pulling in opposite directions. The תרומה ברייתא allows it לכתחילה, and the ברכת המזון ברייתא allows it only בדיעבד. Each view of רבי יהודה leaves one of them without an author. Steps 10 and 12 resolve this.

phrases.english: But rather, what? Rabbi Yehuda
permits it even from the outset too?
But what about that which was taught:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא יְבָרֵךְ אָדָם בִּרְכַּת הַמָּזוֹן בְּלִבּוֹ,
phrases.english: A person should not recite Grace after Meals in his heart,
but if he recited it, he has fulfilled his obligation,
whose view is it?
phrases.notes: The answer comes next.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מַאי, רַבִּי יְהוּדָה וַאֲפִילּוּ לְכַתְּחִלָּה נָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the suggestion from Step 7 that רבי יהודה allows it לכתחילה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The suggestion that רבי יהודה allows words said without hearing even לכתחילה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא rules 'בדיעבד yes, לכתחילה no' for silent ברכת המזון. If רבי יהודה allowed it לכתחילה, no תנא would match that ברייתא.

steps.title: The silent ברכת המזון ruling fits neither רבי יהודה nor רבי יוסי
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא spells out why the ברייתא ('do not say it silently, but if you did, you are יוצא') has no author. רבי יהודה allows it even לכתחילה. רבי יוסי does not allow it even בדיעבד.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not רבי יהודה and not רבי יוסי. If it is רבי יהודה, he said it is fine even לכתחילה! And if it is רבי יוסי, he said it is not good even בדיעבד!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the question from the previous step. It shows that the ברכת המזון ברייתא does not match either opinion we know.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 8 raised the suggestion that רבי יהודה allows a non-hearing recital even לכתחילה. If so, a ruling of 'לכתחילה no, בדיעבד yes' cannot be his. It also cannot be רבי יוסי's, since he says one is not יוצא even after the fact. The ברייתא now looks like it has no author.

keyTerms.meaning: but didn't he say? (pointing to a contradiction)

phrases.aramaic: לָא רַבִּי יְהוּדָה וְלָא רַבִּי יוֹסֵי.
phrases.english: Neither Rabbi Yehuda nor Rabbi Yosei.
If it is Rabbi Yehuda,
didn't he say it is fine even from the outset?
And if it is Rabbi Yosei,

phrases.aramaic: הָא אָמַר אֲפִילּוּ דִּיעֲבַד נָמֵי לָא!
phrases.english: didn't he say it does not work even after the fact!

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא רַבִּי יְהוּדָה וְלָא רַבִּי יוֹסֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the question of step 8 by showing that the ברייתא matches neither known view.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברכת המזון ברייתא (לכתחילה no, בדיעבד yes)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יהודה is more lenient than this ruling (even לכתחילה is fine), and רבי יוסי is stricter (even בדיעבד does not work). The middle position has no author.

steps.title: רבי יהודה's own view versus his teacher's view
steps.stepSummary: The answer: רבי יהודה himself allows it even לכתחילה. The ברכת המזון ברייתא reflects the view of his teacher.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, it is רבי יהודה, and he allows it even לכתחילה. There is no difficulty: this ruling is his own, and that ruling is his teacher's.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the two ברייתות reflect two different people. One is רבי יהודה's own opinion. The other is the opinion of his teacher.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תרומה ברייתא (even לכתחילה) is רבי יהודה's own view. The ברכת המזון ברייתא (לכתחילה no, בדיעבד yes) follows his teacher. So there is no contradiction, because different people hold the two rulings. The next step shows who the teacher is.

phrases.english: Actually, it is Rabbi Yehuda,
and he allows it even from the outset.
And it is not difficult:
this is his own view, that is his teacher's view.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְעוֹלָם רַבִּי יְהוּדָה הִיא, וַאֲפִילּוּ לְכַתְּחִלָּה נָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 9 by giving the two ברייתות to two different people.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Two sources, two authors (student versus teacher)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both ברייתות had to reflect רבי יהודה's single view, so they contradicted each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יהודה himself allows it even לכתחילה (the תרומה ברייתא). The ברכת המזון ברייתא follows his teacher.

steps.title: The ברייתא showing רבי יהודה's teacher and רבי מאיר's disagreement
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה quotes רבי אלעזר בן עזריה: one must make קריאת שמע audible to his own ears, based on 'שמע ישראל'. רבי מאיר disagrees: what counts is the intention of the heart.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: רבי יהודה said in the name of רבי אלעזר בן עזריה: One who reads שמע must make it audible to his ears, as it says 'שמע ישראל' (Hear, Israel). רבי מאיר said to him: But it says 'which I command you today, upon your heart.' The words follow the intention of the heart.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to prove that רבי יהודה had a teacher who held 'לכתחילה, you must hear yourself.' The ברייתא also records רבי מאיר's opposing view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר בן עזריה reads 'שמע' as 'make it heard,' so לכתחילה you must hear yourself. בדיעבד, you are still יוצא. This matches the ברכת המזון ברייתא exactly. רבי מאיר holds that the heart is what matters, so hearing is not needed at all. His view will be used in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: as it was taught (in a ברייתא)
that he make it audible to his own ears

steps.confusionAlert: רבי יהודה is quoting his teacher here. This is רבי אלעזר בן עזריה's view, not necessarily רבי יהודה's own view, and that is exactly the point of the first answer.

phrases.english: As it was taught:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עֲזַרְיָה:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda said in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya:

phrases.aramaic: הַקּוֹרֵא אֶת שְׁמַע צָרִיךְ שֶׁיַּשְׁמִיעַ לְאׇזְנוֹ,
phrases.english: One who reads Shema must make it audible to his ear,
as it says: "Hear, Israel."
Rabbi Meir said to him:
But it says:
"Which I command you today, upon your heart",

phrases.aramaic: אַחַר כַּוָּנַת הַלֵּב הֵן הֵן הַדְּבָרִים.
phrases.english: the words follow the intention of the heart.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא, אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עֲזַרְיָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source for 'his teacher's view' mentioned in step 10.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי יהודה's teacher held 'לכתחילה must hear, בדיעבד יצא'
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא: רבי יהודה quoting רבי אלעזר בן עזריה, with רבי מאיר disagreeing

steps.title: Second answer: the תרומה ruling follows רבי מאיר
steps.stepSummary: Now that the full ברייתא is known, a new answer works. רבי יהודה can agree with his teacher. The ברכת המזון ברייתא is רבי יהודה's, and the תרומה ברייתא (even לכתחילה) is רבי מאיר's.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now that you have come to this, you can even say that רבי יהודה holds like his teacher. It is still not difficult: this ruling is רבי יהודה's, and that ruling is רבי מאיר's.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a different solution using רבי מאיר, who was just introduced in the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first answer, רבי יהודה's own view was 'even לכתחילה.' Now רבי יהודה is said to follow his teacher: לכתחילה no, בדיעבד yes. So the ברכת המזון ברייתא is his. The תרומה ברייתא, which allows a deaf person even לכתחילה, follows רבי מאיר, who says only the heart matters.

keyTerms.meaning: now that you have come to this (a new answer based on new information)

steps.whatToRemember: Two answers: (1) רבי יהודה = even לכתחילה, and the ברכת המזון ברייתא = his teacher רבי אלעזר בן עזריה. (2) רבי יהודה = like his teacher, and the תרומה ברייתא = רבי מאיר.

phrases.english: Now that you have come to this,
you can even say
that Rabbi Yehuda holds like his teacher,
and it is not difficult:

phrases.aramaic: הָא — רַבִּי יְהוּדָה, הָא — רַבִּי מֵאִיר.
phrases.english: this is Rabbi Yehuda, that is Rabbi Meir.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses רבי מאיר from step 11 to give a second answer to the question of step 9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Assigning one ברייתא to a different תנא (רבי מאיר)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only רבי יהודה and רבי יוסי were available as authors, so the two ברייתות clashed.
steps.terutzMaskana: ברכת המזון ברייתא = רבי יהודה (like his teacher). תרומה ברייתא = רבי מאיר (heart alone matters).

steps.title: The הלכה follows רבי יהודה in both statements
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא quoting רב שילא rules that the הלכה follows רבי יהודה quoting רבי אלעזר בן עזריה, and also follows רבי יהודה in our משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said in the name of רב שילא: The הלכה is like רבי יהודה, who spoke in the name of רבי אלעזר בן עזריה. And the הלכה is like רבי יהודה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes the discussion with a practical ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first ruling means that לכתחילה, a person must make קריאת שמע audible to his own ears. The second ruling, following רבי יהודה in our משנה, means that if he did not, he is still יוצא בדיעבד. Together they give the practical rule: say it audibly, but after the fact you are covered.

keyTerms.meaning: the earlier אמורא whose ruling is quoted

steps.whatToRemember: Practical הלכה: לכתחילה, say שמע loud enough to hear yourself. בדיעבד, if you did not, you are still יוצא.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the halachic practice of reciting קריאת שמע audibly while still being יוצא after the fact.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר רַב שֵׁילָא:
phrases.english: Rav Chisda said in the name of Rav Sheila:
The halacha is like Rabbi Yehuda

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאָמַר מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עֲזַרְיָה,
phrases.english: who spoke in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya,
and the halacha is like Rabbi Yehuda (in our Mishna).

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר רַב שֵׁילָא: הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the theoretical answers, gives the practical ruling.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: לכתחילה one must make קריאת שמע audible to his own ears (רבי יהודה quoting רבי אלעזר בן עזריה). בדיעבד he is still יוצא (רבי יהודה in our משנה).

steps.title: Why the second ruling is needed: the first alone sounds too lenient
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that ruling only 'הלכה כרבי יהודה' could be misread as permitting silent קריאת שמע even לכתחילה. So רב חסדא added 'כרבי יהודה משום רבי אלעזר בן עזריה' to show that one must say it audibly from the start.
steps.simpleTranslation: Both rulings are needed. If he had only told us 'the הלכה follows רבי יהודה,' I would have thought it is fine even לכתחילה to say it silently. So he tells us 'the הלכה follows רבי יהודה quoting רבי אלעזר בן עזריה,' meaning you must say it audibly from the start.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers an unspoken question: why did רב חסדא give two rulings that seem to repeat each other? This step explains the first half of the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Back in Steps 8 and 10, the גמרא raised the possibility that רבי יהודה allows silent reading even לכתחילה. If רב חסדא had said only 'הלכה כרבי יהודה,' we could have read it that way. The second ruling, which quotes רבי אלעזר בן עזריה's 'must make it audible,' blocks that reading.

keyTerms.meaning: And it is necessary: the opening word of a צריכותא, which shows that two statements that look the same are both needed
I would have thought (a mistaken first assumption)
From the start; the proper way to act

phrases.english: And it is necessary (to have both rulings),
for if he had only taught us
'the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda,'
I would have said: even from the start (silent reading is fine),
so he teaches us: the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאָמַר מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עֲזַרְיָה.
phrases.english: who said it in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.
phrases.notes: That is, one must make it audible from the start.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the double ruling in Step 13 is not repetitive.
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכותא: shows that each statement is necessary
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A plain 'הלכה כרבי יהודה' might mean silent reading is fine even לכתחילה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The second ruling shows that one must make it audible לכתחילה.

steps.title: Why the first ruling is needed: the second alone sounds too strict
steps.stepSummary: Ruling only like רבי אלעזר בן עזריה could be misread as saying that silent קריאת שמע is invalid even בדיעבד. The plain 'הלכה כרבי יהודה,' which matches the משנה's 'יצא,' shows it is valid after the fact.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if he had only told us 'the הלכה follows רבי יהודה quoting רבי אלעזר בן עזריה,' I would have thought it must be audible and there is no fix if it wasn't. So he tells us 'the הלכה follows רבי יהודה' from our משנה, meaning that after the fact you are יוצא.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the second half of the צריכותא. It shows why the first ruling is also needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'צריך' (must) could mean the reading does not count at all if it wasn't audible. The ruling like רבי יהודה in the משנה, who says 'יצא,' shows that this requirement is only לכתחילה. The two rulings together give the full law: say it audibly from the start, but it still counts after the fact.

keyTerms.meaning: He has no fix; it does not count even after the fact

steps.whatToRemember: The final law for קריאת שמע: say it loud enough to hear yourself לכתחילה, but if you didn't, you are still יוצא בדיעבד.

phrases.english: And if he had only taught us
'the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda'

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאָמַר מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עֲזַרְיָה,
phrases.english: who said it in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya,

phrases.aramaic: הֲוָה אָמֵינָא צָרִיךְ וְאֵין לוֹ תַּקָּנָה.
phrases.english: I would have said: he must (say it audibly), and he has no fix (if he didn't).
So he teaches us: the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda (in our Mishnah, who says he is יוצא).
phrases.notes: Silent reading counts after the fact.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי אַשְׁמְעִינַן הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה שֶׁאָמַר מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עֲזַרְיָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the צריכותא begun in Step 14.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Must be audible' could mean it is invalid even בדיעבד.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ruling like רבי יהודה in the משנה shows it is valid בדיעבד.

steps.title: רב יוסף limits the dispute to קריאת שמע
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף says the argument about not hearing one's own words applies only to קריאת שמע. For all other מצות, everyone agrees one is not יוצא, based on the פסוק 'הסכת ושמע ישראל.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: The argument is only about קריאת שמע. But for other מצות, everyone agrees he is not יוצא, as it says, 'Pay attention and hear, ישראל.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new אמורא, רב יוסף, makes a statement about how far the argument reaches. He says that for other מצות the rule is stricter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף reads 'הסכת ושמע' as a general requirement to hear what you say in every מצוה. According to this version, only קריאת שמע is open to debate, so for other מצות everyone agrees that unheard words don't count.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't memorize this version as the final one. The גמרא will soon reject it and flip רב יוסף's statement.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
The dispute is (only) in reciting Shema,
but in the other מצוות,
everyone agrees he is not יוצא,
as it is written: 'Pay attention and hear, Israel.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: מַחֲלוֹקֶת בִּקְרִיאַת שְׁמַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the ruling on קריאת שמע to the question of other מצות.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In this first version: the dispute is only about קריאת שמע, and in other מצות everyone agrees one is not יוצא without hearing.

steps.title: A ברייתא about ברכת המזון contradicts רב יוסף
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא: one should not say ברכת המזון silently, but if he did, he is יוצא. ברכת המזון is one of the 'other מצות,' yet it counts after the fact.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged him: A person should not say ברכת המזון in his heart, but if he did, he is יוצא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב יוסף with a ברייתא that shows the opposite of what he said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף said that in other מצות everyone agrees one is not יוצא. But this ברייתא is about ברכת המזון, which is not קריאת שמע, and it rules 'יצא.' So his 'everyone agrees' cannot be correct.

keyTerms.meaning: They challenged (usually from a ברייתא or משנה)

phrases.english: They challenged:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא יְבָרֵךְ אָדָם בִּרְכַּת הַמָּזוֹן בְּלִבּוֹ,
phrases.english: A person should not recite Birkat HaMazon in his heart,
but if he did recite it that way, he is יוצא.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵיתִיבִי: לֹא יְבָרֵךְ אָדָם בִּרְכַּת הַמָּזוֹן בְּלִבּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב יוסף's statement in Step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's claim that in other מצות everyone agrees one is not יוצא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: ברכת המזון is one of the 'other מצות,' and the ברייתא says one is יוצא בדיעבד without saying it audibly.

steps.title: רב יוסף's statement is corrected: in other מצות everyone agrees one is יוצא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא corrects the version of רב יוסף's statement. The dispute is only in קריאת שמע because of 'שמע ישראל,' but in other מצות everyone agrees one is יוצא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, if it was said, this is how it was said: רב יוסף said the argument is only about קריאת שמע, because it says 'שמע ישראל.' But for other מצות, everyone agrees he is יוצא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא does not defend the first version. It replaces it with a corrected version of what רב יוסף actually said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling flips. Now קריאת שמע is the stricter case because of its special word 'שמע' (hear), so only there do some say one is not יוצא. In other מצות no such פסוק applies, so everyone agrees one is יוצא, which fits the ברכת המזון ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: If it was said, this is how it was said (a correction of a quoted statement)

steps.whatToRemember: Final version of רב יוסף: the dispute is only in קריאת שמע, because of 'שמע ישראל.' In all other מצות, everyone agrees one is יוצא even without hearing his own words.
steps.confusionAlert: The two versions say opposite things about other מצות. Only the second version, 'יצא,' stands.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the requirement to hear oneself comes from a special word in the פסוק of קריאת שמע, not from a general rule for all spoken מצות.

phrases.english: Rather, if it was said, this is how it was said:
Rav Yosef said:
The dispute is (only) in reciting Shema,
as it is written: 'Hear, Israel,'
but in the other מצוות,
everyone agrees he is יוצא.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the קשיא of Step 17 by correcting the version of Step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Emendation of the אמורא's statement (אי איתמר הכי איתמר)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: In other מצות everyone agrees one is not יוצא without hearing.
steps.terutzMaskana: In other מצות everyone agrees one is יוצא; only קריאת שמע is debated, because of 'שמע ישראל.'
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The dispute about hearing one's own words is limited to קריאת שמע. In other מצות one is יוצא without it.

steps.title: Doesn't 'Pay Attention and Hear' Require Hearing for All מצות?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the corrected version of רב יוסף's statement. The פסוק 'הסכת ושמע ישראל' seems to require hearing one's own words in every מצוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: But isn't it written: 'Pay attention and hear, Israel'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks what it just said. It had concluded that in other מצות everyone agrees one is יוצא even without hearing his own words. Now it points to a פסוק that seems to demand hearing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new version of רב יוסף said that only קריאת שמע has a special source ('שמע ישראל') for the dispute, and other מצות are valid even when said silently. But 'הסכת ושמע ישראל' is a general פסוק that says 'hear.' That seems to require hearing for everything, which would mean that silent ברכת המזון and similar מצות should not count.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it written? (opens a challenge from a פסוק)
Pay attention / be silent and listen

phrases.english: But isn't it written: 'Pay attention and hear, Israel'?
phrases.notes: A פסוק in דברים כ״ז. It is the same פסוק that the first version of רב יוסף used.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the corrected version of רב יוסף given in step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that in other מצות everyone agrees one is יוצא without hearing his own words.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A general פסוק says 'hear,' so hearing seems to be required in all מצות, not only in קריאת שמע.

steps.title: That Verse Is About Learning Torah
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that 'הסכת ושמע ישראל' is talking about דברי תורה, meaning paying careful attention when learning. It is not a rule about saying מצות out loud.
steps.simpleTranslation: That פסוק is written about words of Torah.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends its position. It explains that the פסוק is not about hearing one's own words in a מצוה at all. It is about how to learn Torah.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer limits the scope of the פסוק to Torah study, where one must focus and listen closely. So the פסוק teaches nothing about whether a silent ברכה or other מצוה counts. The corrected version of רב יוסף stands: outside of קריאת שמע, one is יוצא even if he did not hear his words.

keyTerms.meaning: Words of Torah, meaning Torah learning

steps.whatToRemember: Only קריאת שמע has a special source ('שמע ישראל') for the dispute about hearing. 'הסכת ושמע' is about learning Torah. For other מצות, one is יוצא בדיעבד even if he said it silently.

phrases.english: That is written regarding words of Torah.
phrases.notes: It means one must pay close attention when learning Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 19.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the scope of the פסוק to a different subject (Torah study).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'הסכת ושמע ישראל' requires hearing one's own words in all מצות.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק is about focusing while learning Torah. Other מצות are valid even when said silently.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה: Reading Without Care for the Letters
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה. It is about someone who read שמע but was not careful to pronounce its letters clearly.
steps.simpleTranslation: [The משנה said:] 'One who read [שמע] and was not careful with its letters.'
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא quotes a new piece of the משנה to prepare for the ruling that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, רבי יוסי says such a person is יוצא and רבי יהודה says he is not. This is a second dispute, separate from the dispute about not hearing one's own words. In that first dispute the תנא קמא says יצא and רבי יוסי says לא יצא.

keyTerms.meaning: In its letters (clear pronunciation of each letter)

phrases.english: 'One who read and was not precise in its letters.'
phrases.notes: A quote from the משנה. רבי יוסי says יצא and רבי יהודה says לא יצא.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the discussion of hearing and moves to the next clause of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה's case: someone read שמע without pronouncing its letters carefully (a dispute between רבי יוסי and רבי יהודה).

steps.title: The הלכה Follows the Lenient View in Both Disputes
steps.stepSummary: רבי טבי, quoting רבי יאשיה, rules that the הלכה follows the lenient opinion in both disputes of the משנה. Saying שמע without hearing it counts, and saying it without precise letters also counts.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי טבי said in the name of רבי יאשיה: The הלכה follows the words of both of them, to be lenient.
steps.whatsHappening: An אמורא gives a final ruling that covers both disputes in the משנה at once. In each dispute, we follow the opinion that says one is יוצא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the hearing dispute, the lenient view is the תנא קמא, so one who did not hear his own words is יוצא. In the letters dispute, the lenient view is רבי יוסי, so one who was not careful with the letters is יוצא. We take the lenient side of each dispute even though רבי יוסי is lenient in one and strict in the other.
steps.confusionAlert: רבי יוסי appears on opposite sides of the two disputes. He is strict about hearing (לא יצא) but lenient about the letters (יצא). 'Both of them, to be lenient' does not mean 'follow רבי יוסי.' It means: in each dispute, pick whichever opinion is lenient.
steps.whatToRemember: Final ruling: בדיעבד, one is יוצא קריאת שמע even if he did not hear his own words, and even if he was not careful with the letters.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the practical הלכה for both flaws in reading קריאת שמע. It fits the earlier ruling that silent שמע counts after the fact.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי טָבִי אָמַר רַבִּי יֹאשִׁיָּה:
phrases.english: Rabbi Tavi said that Rabbi Yoshiya said:
The halakha follows the words of both of them, to be lenient.
phrases.notes: Hearing: the תנא קמא (יצא). Letters: רבי יוסי (יצא).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the ruling on the משנה clause quoted in step 21, together with the earlier hearing dispute.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In both disputes the הלכה follows the lenient view.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Not hearing one's own words and not pronouncing the letters precisely do not stop one from being יוצא קריאת שמע בדיעבד.

steps.title: The grave is compared to the womb
steps.stepSummary: רבי טבי, quoting רבי יאשיה, asks why a פסוק in משלי places the grave (שאול) next to the womb (רחם). He answers that just as a womb takes in and gives out, the grave also takes in and will give out.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי טבי said in the name of רבי יאשיה: What does the פסוק mean when it says 'There are three things that are never satisfied... the grave and the closed womb'? What does a grave have to do with a womb? Rather, it comes to teach you: just as a womb takes in and gives out, so too a grave takes in and gives out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second teaching from the same pair of רבנן it just quoted. This one is about a פסוק that hints at תחיית המתים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק lists the grave and the womb side by side, which seems strange. רבי יאשיה says the pairing teaches a shared quality: a womb takes something in and later brings out a living child. So the grave, which takes in the dead, will also one day bring them back out alive.

keyTerms.meaning: What does this have to do with that? (asks why two things are paired)

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי טָבִי אָמַר רַבִּי יֹאשִׁיָּה:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Tavi said in the name of Rabbi Yoshiya:
phrases.notes: Same pair of Rabbis as the ruling in the previous step, so the גמרא adds another teaching of theirs.

phrases.english: What is the meaning of what is written:
'There are three things that are never satisfied...'
phrases.notes: משלי ל:טו-טז

phrases.english: '...the grave and the barren womb.'

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי מָה עִנְיַן שְׁאוֹל אֵצֶל רֶחֶם?
phrases.english: What does a grave have to do with a womb?
Rather, it comes to tell you:
Just as a womb takes in and gives out,
so too a grave takes in and gives out.
phrases.notes: A hint to תחיית המתים.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי טָבִי אָמַר רַבִּי יֹאשִׁיָּה: מַאי דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brought only because it comes from the same pair of רבנן (רבי טבי and רבי יאשיה) quoted in step 22. It is a side topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Placing the grave next to the womb teaches that the grave, like the womb, will 'give back' what it receives. This hints at תחיית המתים.

steps.title: A קל וחומר proves the dead will rise
steps.stepSummary: רבי יאשיה strengthens his point with a קל וחומר. If a womb, where things go in quietly, gives out with loud noise, then surely the grave, where things go in with loud crying, will give out with loud noise. This answers those who say תחיית המתים is not from the Torah.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't this a קל וחומר? A womb: things go into it quietly, yet a baby comes out of it with loud cries. The grave: things go into it with loud cries of mourning. Isn't it logical that they will come out of it with loud sounds too? From here is an answer to those who say תחיית המתים is not from the Torah.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יאשיה adds a logical argument, a קל וחומר, to make his reading of the פסוק stronger. He then states what it proves: תחיית המתים has a source in the Torah.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The womb is the 'weaker' case: what goes in comes in silently, yet it still gives out loudly. The grave is the 'stronger' case: the dead go in with loud mourning. So the grave should surely give out loudly too, meaning the dead will come back to life.

keyTerms.meaning: A logical argument from a weaker case to a stronger case
Isn't it logical? (the conclusion of a קל וחומר)

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יאשיה learns from 'grave next to womb' plus a קל וחומר that the grave will give back the dead. This answers those who deny that תחיית המתים is from the Torah.

phrases.english: And isn't this a kal vachomer?
If a womb, which things are put into quietly,
gives things out with loud cries,
phrases.notes: The cries of childbirth.

phrases.english: then the grave, which things are put into with loud cries,
phrases.notes: The cries of mourning at a burial.

phrases.aramaic: אֵינוֹ דִין שֶׁמּוֹצִיאִין מִמֶּנּוּ בְּקוֹלֵי קוֹלוֹת?
phrases.english: isn't it logical that it gives them out with loud sounds?
From here is an answer to those who say
that resurrection of the dead is not from the Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Strengthens the reading in step 23 with a קל וחומר and states what it proves.
steps.raayaObject: That תחיית המתים has a source in the Torah (the whole תנ"ך, here משלי).
steps.raayaSupportSource: The pairing of שאול and רחם in משלי, plus a קל וחומר from womb to grave.

steps.title: Everything must be written, even the commands
steps.stepSummary: רבי אושעיא teaches a ברייתא in front of רבא. The word 'וכתבתם' teaches that everything in the פרשה must be written, even the command sections.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אושעיא taught in front of רבא: 'And you shall write them' teaches that everything must be in writing, even the commands.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the פרשיות of קריאת שמע and brings a ברייתא about writing them in מזוזה and תפילין. It says the whole text must be written, with nothing left out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One might think only the main content needs to be written, and not the instruction lines like 'write them on your doorposts.' The ברייתא learns from 'וכתבתם' that even those command lines must be written.

keyTerms.meaning: And you shall write them (דברים ו:ט)

phrases.english: Rabbi Oshaya taught in front of Rava:
'And you shall write them'
phrases.notes: Said about מזוזה (and similarly תפילין).

phrases.english: everything must be in writing, even the commands.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The side topic is finished. The גמרא returns to הלכות related to the פרשיות of קריאת שמע.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The word 'וכתבתם' requires writing the entire פרשה in מזוזה and תפילין, including the command lines.

steps.title: רבא says this ברייתא follows רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: רבא tells רבי אושעיא that this ברייתא follows רבי יהודה. רבי יהודה holds that in the סוטה scroll the כהן writes only the curses, not the commands.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: Who taught you this? It is רבי יהודה. He said about סוטה that the כהן writes the curses but does not write the commands.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא identifies whose opinion the ברייתא follows. He links it to רבי יהודה's ruling about the scroll written for a סוטה, and this sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By סוטה, the כהן writes a scroll and dissolves it in water. רבי יהודה says only the curse lines go into that scroll, not the instruction lines. Since רבי יהודה distinguishes between curses and commands there, the 'even the commands' in the ברייתא sounds like his way of thinking.

keyTerms.meaning: Who is it? (asks whose opinion a teaching follows)
A woman suspected by her husband of unfaithfulness, who drinks the special waters

steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not arguing with the ברייתא. He is only identifying which תנא it follows.

phrases.english: He (Rava) said to him: Who is the one who told you this?
It is Rabbi Yehuda,
who said regarding a sota:
he writes the curses, but he does not write the commands.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לֵיהּ: דַּאֲמַר לָךְ מַנִּי — רַבִּי יְהוּדָה הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Identifies the author of the ברייתא from step 25.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ברייתא follows רבי יהודה, who distinguishes curses from commands in the סוטה scroll.

steps.title: Different verses lead to different rules
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that by סוטה the פסוק says 'he shall write these curses', so only curses are written. By מזוזה it says 'וכתבתם', so even the commands are written.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, by סוטה, it is written 'And he shall write these curses', so only the curses. But here, where it is written 'And you shall write them', even the commands are included.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא finishes his point by showing why רבי יהודה rules differently in the two cases. Each rule comes from the exact wording of its own פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The סוטה פסוק names its content, 'these curses', which limits what is written. The מזוזה פסוק says only 'write them', with no limit, so it includes the whole פרשה. Because רבי יהודה reads the סוטה פסוק so precisely, the contrast fits his view.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי יהודה, the סוטה scroll has only the curses because its פסוק says 'these curses'. מזוזה and תפילין include everything, even the commands, because their פסוק says simply 'וכתבתם'.

phrases.english: And there it is written:
'And he shall write these curses'
phrases.notes: במדבר ה:כג. The wording limits it to curses.

phrases.english: but here, where it is written 'And you shall write them',
even the commands are also included.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבא's attribution from step 26 by explaining the textual difference between סוטה and מזוזה.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: For רבי יהודה, the wording of each פסוק decides what is written. In סוטה only the curses are written. In מזוזה and תפילין everything is written, including the commands.

steps.title: רבי יהודה's real reason comes from the word 'curses'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבא's explanation. רבי יהודה's limit for סוטה comes from the word אָלוֹת (curses), not from the word וְכָתַב.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is רבי יהודה's reason really because the פסוק says 'he shall write'? His reason is because the פסוק says 'curses': curses are written, commands are not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רבא's contrast between וְכָתַב (סוטה) and וּכְתַבְתָּם (מזוזה). It says the real reason only curses are written in a סוטה scroll is the word אָלוֹת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the limit for סוטה comes from the word אָלוֹת, then the word וְכָתַב by itself does not limit anything. So for מזוזה, where there is no limiting word, we would write everything anyway. Then why do we need the extra word וּכְתַבְתָּם?

keyTerms.meaning: Is that to say? (introduces a challenge)

steps.confusionAlert: The question is not against רבי יהודה's ruling. It is a question about why the word וּכְתַבְתָּם is needed for מזוזה, if the limit by סוטה comes from a different word.

phrases.english: Is that to say Rabbi Yehuda's reason
is because it is written "and he shall write"?
Rabbi Yehuda's reason
is because it is written "curses."
Curses, yes; commands, no.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַטּוּ טַעְמֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה מִשּׁוּם דִּכְתִיב וְכָתַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's contrast between וְכָתַב and וּכְתַבְתָּם from Step 27.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's claim that the word וּכְתַבְתָּם is what teaches that commands are written in a מזוזה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The limit for סוטה comes from the word אָלוֹת. So with no such limit by מזוזה, everything would be written anyway, and וּכְתַבְתָּם seems unnecessary.

steps.title: The word וּכְתַבְתָּם is needed to block a גזירה שוה
steps.stepSummary: וּכְתַבְתָּם is needed. Otherwise we would learn 'writing' by מזוזה from 'writing' by סוטה, and leave out the commands there too.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was needed. You might have thought to learn 'writing' from 'writing' there: just as there curses are written and commands are not, so too here commands are not written. So the Torah wrote וּכְתַבְתָּם, meaning even the commands.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. Without the word וּכְתַבְתָּם, we would have compared מזוזה to סוטה because both use the word 'writing', and copied the limit from סוטה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A גזירה שוה links two places that use the same word, so the rule of one carries over to the other. Since סוטה says 'writing' and only curses are written there, we might have limited מזוזה the same way. The full form וּכְתַבְתָּם tells us to write the whole פרשה, commands included.

keyTerms.meaning: it might have entered your mind to say
'writing' from 'writing' (a גזירה שוה using the shared word)

steps.whatToRemember: וּכְתַבְתָּם is not extra. It stops us from copying the סוטה limit over to מזוזה, so a מזוזה must contain the entire פרשה, even the commands.

phrases.english: It was necessary,
because it might have entered your mind to say
let us derive "writing" from "writing" there:

phrases.aramaic: מָה הָתָם — אָלוֹת אִין, צַוָּאוֹת לָא.
phrases.english: just as there, curses yes, commands no,
so too here, commands no.
So the Torah wrote "and you shall write them":
even the commands.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 28.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains why the פסוק is needed: it blocks a mistaken גזירה שוה.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Learn מזוזה from סוטה through the shared word 'writing', so only part of the פרשה would be written.
steps.terutzMaskana: וּכְתַבְתָּם teaches that the whole פרשה, including the commands, is written in a מזוזה.

steps.title: Your learning must be 'complete': pause between words that run together
steps.stepSummary: רב עובדיה teaches before רבא that וְלִמַּדְתֶּם means your learning must be תָּם (complete). A person must leave a gap between words that stick together.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב עובדיה taught before רבא: 'And you shall teach them' (וְלִמַּדְתֶּם) means your learning should be complete (תָּם). You must leave space between words that stick together.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about reading קריאת שמע. It reads the word וְלִמַּדְתֶּם as 'לִמּוּד תָּם' (complete learning), which means saying each word clearly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like the earlier teachings on 'וכתבתם', this ברייתא reads a word from שמע to teach a new rule. Here the rule is about speaking, not writing. When one word ends with the same sound the next word starts with, you must pause so the two words do not blend.

keyTerms.meaning: words that stick together (one ends with the letter the next begins with)

phrases.english: Rav Ovadya taught before Rava:
"And you shall teach them": that your teaching should be complete,
that one should leave space between words that stick together.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new ברייתא with a similar style: another wording-based teaching from the פרשיות of שמע.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In קריאת שמע, a person must pause between adjacent words where one word ends with the same letter the next begins with.

steps.title: רבא lists examples of words that run together
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains רב עובדיה's rule by listing word pairs in קריאת שמע that could blend together.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא answered after him: for example, על לבבך, על לבבכם, בכל לבבך, בכל לבבכם, עשב בשדך, ואבדתם מהרה, הכנף פתיל, אתכם מארץ.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא adds to רב עובדיה's teaching by giving real examples from קריאת שמע. In each pair, the last letter of the first word matches the first letter of the next word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא is not arguing. He is showing exactly where the rule applies. For example, 'בְּכָל לְבָבְךָ' ends in ל and starts with ל, and 'עֵשֶׂב בְּשָׂדְךָ' ends in ב and starts with ב. If you do not pause, the two words merge and the meaning gets lost.

keyTerms.meaning: 'the corner, a thread': ends in פ / פ, from the ציצית section

steps.whatToRemember: When saying קריאת שמע, pause slightly between words where the same sound ends one word and begins the next, like 'בְּכָל לְבָבְךָ' and 'עֵשֶׂב בְּשָׂדְךָ', so every word is clear.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a practical הלכה followed every day when saying שמע: careful, clear pronunciation of each word.

phrases.english: Rava responded after him:
For example, "al levavekha," "al levavkhem,"
"bekhol levavekha," "bekhol levavkhem,"
"esev besadkha," "va'avadtem mehera,"
"hakanaf petil," "etkhem me'eretz."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives concrete examples of the rule taught in Step 30.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: These pairs in קריאת שמע need a pause between them: על לבבך, על לבבכם, בכל לבבך, בכל לבבכם, עשב בשדך, ואבדתם מהרה, הכנף פתיל, אתכם מארץ.

steps.title: Careful pronunciation of שמע cools גיהנם
steps.stepSummary: רבי חמא ברבי חנינא teaches that whoever says קריאת שמע and pronounces its letters precisely has גיהנם cooled for him. He proves it by re-reading two words in a פסוק in תהלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חמא ברבי חנינא said: Anyone who says קריאת שמע and is careful with its letters will have גיהנם cooled for him. The פסוק says: 'When the Almighty scatters (בְּפָרֵשׂ) kings over it, it will snow in Tzalmon (בְּצַלְמוֹן).' Do not read בְּפָרֵשׂ ('scatters'). Read it as בְּפָרֵשׁ ('pronounces clearly'). Do not read בְּצַלְמוֹן ('in Tzalmon'). Read it as בְּצַלְמָוֶת ('in the shadow of death', meaning גיהנם). So when a person pronounces clearly, God makes it 'snow' in גיהנם for him and cools it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new statement that gives the reward for the careful reading described in the steps just before this one. Then it shows where in the פסוקים this reward is hinted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 30–31 told us how to read קריאת שמע carefully. This step adds what you get for doing it: גיהנם is cooled for you. The proof is an אל תקרי, a creative re-reading. 'Scatters' becomes 'pronounces clearly,' and 'Tzalmon' becomes 'shadow of death,' so the snow falls on גיהנם.

keyTerms.meaning: Careful with its letters. This means pronouncing each letter of קריאת שמע exactly and clearly.
They cool גיהנם for him. His punishment there is softened.
Do not read it as X, but as Y. This is a creative re-reading of a פסוק used to find a hidden lesson. It does not change the actual text.
When one pronounces clearly. This is the re-reading of בְּפָרֵשׂ ('when He scatters').
The shadow of death. Here it is understood as גיהנם.

steps.confusionAlert: אל תקרי does not mean the פסוק is spelled wrong or should be read differently in davening. It is a דרש technique that uses a similar-sounding word to reveal a hidden message. The plain meaning of the פסוק stays the same.
steps.whyThisMatters: The re-reading itself depends on a single letter: שׂ becomes שׁ. So the proof teaches the lesson it is proving. One small letter changes the whole meaning, and that is exactly why you must pronounce every letter of קריאת שמע carefully.

phrases.english: Rabbi Ḥama, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, said:
Anyone who recites Shema
and is precise in pronouncing its letters,
Gehinnom is cooled for him,
as it is stated:
phrases.notes: Introduces the source, תהלים 68:15.

phrases.english: "When the Almighty scatters kings over it,
it will snow in Tzalmon" —
do not read 'befares' (scatters) but 'befaresh' (pronounces clearly),
phrases.notes: The letter changes from שׂ (sin) to שׁ (shin). The new reading means: when one pronounces the Name of the Almighty clearly.

phrases.english: do not read 'beTzalmon' (in Tzalmon) but 'betzalmavet' (in the shadow of death).
phrases.notes: The shadow of death means גיהנם. Snow there means it is cooled.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חָמָא בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא: כָּל הַקּוֹרֵא קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע וּמְדַקְדֵּק בְּאוֹתִיּוֹתֶיהָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Steps 30–31 taught how to read קריאת שמע precisely. This step adds the reward for doing so and brings a פסוק as its source.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Whoever says קריאת שמע and pronounces its letters precisely has גיהנם cooled for him. This is derived from an אל תקרי re-reading of תהלים 68:15.

steps.title: A new teaching begins: why were two topics placed side by side
steps.stepSummary: רבי חמא ברבי חנינא starts a second teaching. He asks why two subjects were placed next to each other. This passage stops before we learn which subjects or the answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי חמא ברבי חנינא also said: Why were they placed next to each other...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a new teaching from the same רבי חמא ברבי חנינא. His question about why two things are placed next to each other is only started here. It will be completed on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word וְאָמַר ('and he also said') shows that this is another statement from the same speaker as Step 32. The question 'why were they placed next to each other' is a common way to learn a lesson from the order of פסוקים or topics. Here it is only an opening line, so we must wait for the next passage to see what is being compared.

keyTerms.meaning: And he also said. This introduces another teaching from the same speaker.
Why were they placed next to each other? This is a question that learns a lesson from which topics or פסוקים appear side by side.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Ḥama, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, also said:
Why were [they] placed next to each other
phrases.notes: The sentence continues on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי חָמָא בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא: לָמָּה נִסְמְכוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This is a second teaching from the same speaker as Step 32. It opens a new topic based on why two subjects are placed side by side.
